<reason>B built the stronger comparative case for selective expansion through diversification and renewal. It directly explained why cheap discovery cannot always substitute for mid-budget execution and why disciplined selection can coexist with increased spending. A raised legitimate marketing costs and the burden to justify additional investment, but relied heavily on unsupported claims about capped audience demand, acquisition savings, and the segment’s uniformly poor returns. B did not establish the optimal allocation, but its mechanisms and responses were more persuasive than A’s repeated insistence on numerical proof.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s answer to the hit-rate challenge identified the missing success payoffs and sequel benchmark: production and marketing costs alone cannot yield the demanded threshold. A subsequently characterized this justified refusal to invent a number as evasion rather than repairing the comparison.</best_rebuttal>
